newsitem.title: SPAIN: Clinton avoids comment on U.S. Senate China probe.
newsitem.headline: Clinton avoids comment on U.S. Senate China probe.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Tuesday declined comment on a U.S. Senate probe into possible illegal campaign contributions by China, saying he was too busy at the NATO summit to follow its developments.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee chairman Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, began the long-awaited televised hearings with a statement that Beijing's communist leaders had a plan to build political influence in the United States through donations.

After remarks to U.S. Embassy staff in Madrid after the first day of a NATO meeting in which leaders invited Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance, Clinton was asked for his thoughts on the investigation -- which critics call a political witchhunt against him.

"I have no comment," Clinton said, adding that he did not even know the details of the first day if hearings. They included accusations that Chinese officials had tried to illegally send money into Democratic Party coffers for last year's elections.
"I can't comment on it," Clinton said. "I've been working here."

Samuel Berger, the White House national security adviser, also declined to discuss the allegations raised at the Senate hearing. "This is a matter that is under investigation," said Berger, saying it would be improper for him to comment.
Allegations were raised late last year that the Chinese government may have violated U.S. election laws by illegally funnelling money to Clinton's Democratic Party.
The Justice Department has launched an investigation into the allegation, but has yet to release its findings.
China has vigorously denied the accusations, saying they were being spread by critics out to discredit Beijing.
